claims.text: Incrementally increasing phosphorus content in a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy will improve glass-forming ability.
Incrementally increasing phosphorus content will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
Higher phosphorus content will produce a more robust and interconnected amorphous network.
Increasing phosphorus content enhances the negative mixing enthalpy.
Increasing phosphorus content may increase atomic-size mismatch.
The deeper negative mixing enthalpy caused by additional phosphorus stabilizes atomic-scale disorder.
Suppression of nucleation kinetics delays crystallization.
The phosphorus-enriched alloy will have a higher glass-transition temperature than the baseline alloy.
The phosphorus-enriched alloy will have a larger heat-capacity jump at the glass transition than the baseline alloy.
The phosphorus-enriched alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the baseline alloy.
The beneficial effect of increasing phosphorus exists only within a limited phosphorus-concentration range.
Excess phosphorus may cause phase separation.
The intervention depends on maintaining configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy near values favorable for a homogeneous amorphous structure.
Cooling rate can alter alloy phase composition and resulting mechanical properties.

contradictions.description: For normalized alloy compositions, phosphorus atomic fraction cannot be increased while the concentrations of every other element remain fixed. The boundary instead calls for maintaining comparable ratios of the other elements, which would require their individual atomic fractions to decrease proportionally.
